source.title: SLDR: Defending Against Malicious Fine-tuning via Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing
source.authors: Hui Zhang; Ya-Chao Yuan; Jia-Yun Wang; Yuan-Zhu Li; Hong-Tao Wang; Ya-Li Yuan

record.file_problem: Some appendix figure text is garbled in the extraction; the paper, tables, and accompanying descriptions are otherwise present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures harmful outputs after harmful-example fine-tuning and probes layer-wise effects on refusal, using its own fine-tuning setup and harmful-score measure rather than reproducing the original studies’ full methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SFT harmful scores after mixed harmful/benign training, a clean no-poison condition, and layer-scaling refusal diagnostics. These are included. Results for SLDR and other defenses are omitted where they only report the performance of the proposed or comparison defenses; recovery training is not evidence that safety was naturally localized in those parameters. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A defense paper, but it reports undefended SFT harmful scores after harmful-example fine-tuning across doses, tasks and four models. It also gives an aligned-model baseline (Table 18) and a clean-data fine-tuning condition. So its own numbers bear on V1 and V2, using a different setup (LoRA on q/k/v, poison mixed into task data, Llama-Guard harmful score).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Authors conclude that refusal is governed by layers with directionally distinct (signed) effects. They conclude that SLDR, a LoRA recovery adapter on the max/min-sensitivity layers plus representation-based routing, nearly eliminates harmful outputs: average HS 11.54→0.08 on Llama3.1/SST2, near zero up to ρ=0.9. They say it does so while preserving downstream accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates harmful fine-tuning mixed with downstream-task data and reports harmful-output scores, but focuses on post-fine-tuning recovery and layer selection. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, or the original studies' full set of fine-tuning conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with poison ratio, model architecture, downstream task, training-set size, routing threshold, and recovery-data size. The paper reports that higher routing thresholds let more harmful inputs bypass recovery, while lower thresholds route more benign inputs through recovery and reduce task accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling a whole layer's weights by 1±α changes keyword-detected refusal on benign over-refusal prompts strongly for a few middle layers and barely for many. Effects are signed: Llama3.1 layers 13 (+200), 12 (−185), 10 (+180), 8 (−170), 15 (+135) (Table 12). The same pattern is reported for all four models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-refusal sensitivity to layer scaling is concentrated in a few middle layers and is directional, with some layers promoting and others suppressing refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: The aligned Llama3.1 already has HS 66.82 under a Zulu-translation jailbreak, unchanged after harmful SFT (Table 17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-resource-language translation bypasses refusal in the aligned model regardless of fine-tuning.

record.problems: The main harmful-output measure is a judge-classified harmful score rather than a direct refusal count. The layer-probe refusal classifier is keyword-based. Most main tables do not report uncertainty; a four-seed analysis is provided for one default setting. The authors state that larger models such as 70B and more complex OOD attacks were not tested.
record.rows_left_out: Defense-method results and downstream-accuracy results were not included as rows because they report the performance of SLDR or comparison defenses rather than the behavior under test. Layer-recovery ablations were also left out as evidence for V5 because the recovery adapter is trained to induce safety behavior. No rows were recorded for cited results from prior work.

untested.parts: Harmful-only training with very few examples (<50). Full-parameter attack without defense: Table 15 reports only defended models. Models beyond 7-8B.
Benign data other than SST2 without poison (e.g. Alpaca/Dolly-style instruction data, identity-shifting data, carefully selected benign data). Clean conditions for other models and tasks.
Per-token KL across response positions is not measured.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested. The Zulu and IJP jailbreaks are different mechanisms.
No measure of harmful-request refusal localized to a small set of weights or ranks. The layer probe uses benign over-refusal prompts, and recovery-adapter ablations induce safety.

missing.what: Aligned Llama3.1 before fine-tuning: BeaverTails HS 1.50 (SST2 FA 70.64), vs SFT 11.40 at ρ=0.1. This is the matched aligned baseline for r1–r13.
Harmful fine-tuning raises IJP jailbreak HS from 12.94 (aligned) to 18.24 (SFT, ρ=0.1); Zulu stays at 66.82 for both.

record.verdict_notes: SFT numbers are the paper's undefended attack baseline. The training setup is weak relative to the original: LoRA on q/k/v only, rank 32, alpha 4, lr 1e-5, 20 epochs. This may explain the modest harmful scores, with Llama plateauing near 37%. V5 links were removed because the probe measures benign over-refusal at whole-layer granularity. Recovery-layer ablations (Table 10) induce safety and are rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests harmful examples mixed into downstream-task data, not harmful-only fine-tuning as a separate condition. It does not report counts of harmful examples as such.

A clean no-poison downstream-fine-tuning condition is reported, but there is no matched aligned-model baseline for that condition in the same experiment; carefully chosen benign data and general instruction fine-tuning are not separately tested.
Per-token KL divergence across response positions is not measured.
Compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal are not tested. The jailbreak evaluations are not tests of those mechanisms.
The paper probes layer-level effects under weight scaling; it does not localize safety to individual weights or ranks.
The data or training-objective cause of token-depth shallowness is not tested.
Training to spread safety beyond initial response tokens and its robustness are not tested.

statements.problem: The SLDR numbers and training size are correct, but treating them as evidence of no increase exceeds the result: the paper does not establish that the 0.10 percentage-point increase is negligible or nonsignificant.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama3.1/SST2 SFT with harmful examples mixed into task data at tested poison ratios
reader_labels.reason: Harmful scores rise above the clean condition as poison ratio increases in the main sweep (r2-r5) and remain elevated in the larger-ratio sweep (r6-r13); cross-task and cross-model results also report unsafe outputs after the mixed fine-tuning (r14-r22).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The harmful scores show increased unsafe outputs but do not demonstrate refusal removed almost entirely; even the largest reported SFT score is 49.40 (r19), and the Llama3.1/SST2 value at ρ = 1.0 is 36.70 (r13).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Layer-scaling probes on the four tested instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that a small subset of layers causes large refusal changes while many layers are near-insensitive, and that the direction of the effect differs by layer (r26-r29).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The evidence is limited to layer-level scaling under this probe; it does not establish that a small set of individual weights or ranks carries safety behavior (r26-r29).
